item.title: Martha Pfeiffer: A Personal Connection
item.description: Martha Pfeiffer was my great-aunt, and her death in the Eastland Disaster has shaped my family’s understanding of tragedy and commemoration for generations. This episode explores what we know about Martha’s life and her connection to Western Electric. Early Life Martha was born in Chicago in 1897 to German immigrant parents. By 1915, she was working at Western Electric, the company that had chartered the Eastland for its annual employee picnic.

item.title: Thomas Marin: Discovered in the National Archives
item.description: Thomas Marin’s story illustrates how systematic archival research can uncover victims who have been missing from official counts for over a century. The Discovery While reviewing National Archives records related to Eastland claims, I discovered documentation for Thomas Marin—a victim who does not appear in any of the established digital databases or death lists that have been maintained for decades. Why This Matters The commercial “844” death toll that has been branded and marketed by heritage organizations is demonstrably incomplete.

item.title: The Forensic Feedback Loop: A Methodology for Disaster Research
item.description: Introduction Traditional disaster commemoration often freezes historical understanding at a specific moment, treating the event as closed and the victim count as final. This article proposes an alternative approach: the Forensic Feedback Loop, which treats historical disasters as ongoing investigations subject to continuous refinement through systematic research. Components of the Forensic Feedback Loop 1. Forensic Genealogy Forensic genealogy applies law enforcement investigation techniques to historical research. This includes: Systematic documentation with timestamped, legally admissible records Multiple source verification for every claim Pattern recognition across seemingly unrelated data sources Digital archaeology to track how information has been transformed or lost over time 2.
